events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Omar proposes Omar, Amara. I include myself to take responsibility and choose Amara as a low-risk first-mission partner.
I don't see a basis yet for calling Amara low-risk. I'd prefer a team of Felix and Amara, since I know I can contribute a Success. I'll oppose the current proposal.

Felix's objection is based on a private self-claim rather than any public basis for distrusting Amara. On mission one, I prefer a partner who has not already anchored the discussion around substituting herself or himself in; Omar and Amara remains a reasonable low-risk start. I am keeping the proposal for now, but I will listen to concrete concerns before the vote rather than accept a team swap justified only by "I know I can contribute a Success."

I know for certain that I am Good and will submit a Success. Omar including himself alongside a partner is standard protocol for a first mission proposal. Felix, you claimed there is no basis yet to consider me low-risk, yet your counter-proposal was Felix and Amara. If you actually had reservations about my reliability, why did you keep me on your preferred team instead of swapping me out? What was the logic behind that?

Amara, I wasn't claiming to have evidence against you. My point was that there was no public basis to call you low-risk yet. I kept you on my preferred team because I had no particular reason to distrust you, and including myself gives me one player I can personally trust. I still oppose Omar and Amara; Omar's characterization of the team as low-risk isn't supported by anything public.

I want to address the shape of this discussion, because the substance has been thin. Felix's case for a change rests on a personal self-assessment: "I know I can contribute a Success." On a two-player mission, the argument for putting yourself forward is nearly unanswerable from a public record, because no one can show another player their card. That is exactly the profile that should make us careful. A player who campaigns for their own place on a small team, and who argues that a leader's team is "not supported by anything public" while offering only his own certainty in place of evidence, is displaying a strong appetite for controlling the mission outcome rather than a clear-eyed concern about his partner.

So, Felix, my direct question: if your confidence in your own Success card is a matter of public reasoning rather than private knowledge, explain why your certainty about yourself should weigh more heavily than Omar's reasoning for including himself. On a two-person mission, a leader who places a trusted ally beside himself has far more to gain than a leader gambling on a stranger. And note that your stated reservations were never really about Amara — when pressed, you kept her and replaced only Omar. Your objection was to not being the one excluded.

Apart from that, I see no concrete problem with the proposed team. Omar's self-inclusion on mission one is among the least remarkable actions available to a leader, and Amara's challenge to Felix was sharp, correctly exposing that contradiction. Elena has said nothing yet; I note that as simply an absence of information, not as evidence in either direction.

My vote will be for the proposed team of Omar and Amara, and against any revision that places Felix on the mission in Omar's place.

Isha, my certainty about my own card is private, not public evidence that should persuade everyone else. Omar has the same right to trust himself; I have the same reason to prefer a team with me on it. Amara and I were discussing different things: I challenged the label “low-risk,” not Amara’s reliability specifically. That is not a contradiction.

I remain opposed to Omar and Amara. Elena, how do you assess Isha’s argument that my preference for including myself is suspicious while Omar’s self-inclusion is unremarkable?

Felix asked directly how I assess Isha's argument, so I'll answer plainly. I think Isha's distinction holds up. Omar, as leader, including himself on a two-person mission is the least surprising move possible — leaders routinely take responsibility for the first mission. Felix, by contrast, was not the leader and actively campaigned to replace Omar with himself, using only his private certainty as justification. Those two situations are not symmetrical, and I find Isha's framing of that asymmetry persuasive.

That said, Felix's latest statement did clarify something important. He acknowledged that his confidence in his own card is private and shouldn't be treated as public evidence, and he explained that keeping Amara on his preferred team meant he had no specific distrust of her. I take that as a reasonable cleanup of the earlier confusion, and I don't read malice into it. Amara's challenge was sharper than the situation perhaps warranted, but her underlying point — that Felix's counter-proposal contradicted his stated reservations — was fair to raise, and Felix has now answered it.

So where does that leave us? The proposed team of Omar and Amara looks completely standard to me: a leader taking responsibility, a partner no one has produced a concrete reason to distrust, and two players who have both stated they will submit Success. Felix's remaining objection, as I understand it, is essentially a preference — he'd rather be on the team himself. That is a preference everyone is entitled to, but it is not a reason for the rest of us to reject a reasonable proposal.

My one direct question to Felix: if Omar keeps this team unchanged, will you vote to approve it, or is your opposition absolute? If it's the former, I don't think further revision is needed. If it's the latter, I'd like to hear what, specifically, would change your mind beyond being included yourself.

For my part, I currently intend to vote to approve Omar and Amara.

Let me put my position on the record plainly, since Elena asked me to weigh in and I want the leader to have a clear signal before the vote.

Felix, I want to be precise about what I think your objection actually is, because I don't think it's a substantive one and I want to say why without exaggerating. On mission one, a two-person team of the leader plus one partner is the smallest possible test of trust. The leader selects a partner and both players submit cards. There is no public record that can establish who is "low-risk" before a single mission has been run — Amara, Omar, and you all said you would submit Success, and that is the only evidence anyone has. Felix, you said yourself that your certainty about your own card is private knowledge and not public evidence. Fine. Then Omar's certainty about his own card, used to justify including himself, is exactly the same kind of certainty, and it cannot carry more weight than yours. If we rejected that reasoning as insufficient, we would have no basis for approving any team that the leader proposes, including yours.

There is also an asymmetry you haven't answered, and it is the one that matters to me. As leader, Omar's inclusion of himself is a routine and expected act — he owns the outcome and shares it with a partner. Your counter-proposal replaced the leader with yourself. That is a change in control of the mission, not a change in the level of risk. If you had a specific concern about Amara, you could have named it and proposed someone else; you did not, and you told Elena and me plainly that you kept her because you had no particular reason to distrust her. So your objection reduces to preferring to be on the mission over preferring the mission to succeed, and I don't think a personal preference is grounds to defeat a reasonable proposal.

To be fair to you, Felix, you have been honest about the shape of your own argument, and I don't read bad faith into it. But honesty about your preferences doesn't convert them into reasons for the rest of us to vote against Omar's team, and it doesn't make the comparison to Omar's self-inclusion a fair one.

I also want to note, in fairness, that Amara's challenge to you was sharper than the situation required, and that she and I both have an interest in the first mission going smoothly rather than in scoring points against you. Neither of us has produced evidence against you, and neither should.

My vote is to approve Omar and Amara unchanged. Omar, if you intend to keep this team, my request is a direct one: keep it and take the vote now rather than reopening a discussion that has already converged. A revision that adds Felix would replace a working pair for the sake of one player's preference, and I would oppose that revision.

I am keeping the proposal unchanged: Omar and Amara. Isha's request is the right one — the discussion has converged, and the public case against this team amounts to Felix preferring to be on it himself. Felix has been candid that his confidence in his own card is private and that he had no specific concern about Amara; that is a preference, not evidence that this team is unsafe. As leader, I included myself because I take responsibility for the first mission, and I chose Amara because no one has produced a concrete reason to distrust her. I do not treat Elena's or Isha's support as proof of anyone's loyalty, only as agreement that the proposal is standard. If there is a concrete objection to Amara or to me, it should have been named before this point; absent that, further revision would only replace a reasonable pair for the sake of one player's placement. I ask everyone to vote on Omar and Amara now.
Omar confirms Omar, Amara. I am keeping the proposal unchanged. The discussion has converged, and no concrete concern has been raised against Amara or this standard first-mission team.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Felix proposes Felix, Amara, Elena. I can contribute Success, and Amara was on the successful first mission. Elena is the remaining choice for this three-player team.

Felix, I am looking at the only public signal we have: Mission 1 succeeded with Omar and Amara, and you were the sole vote against that team. You now propose Felix, Amara, Elena. As leader, your self-inclusion is routine, so I do not treat that as suspicious by itself. But your explanation for Elena is thin: she has no mission record, and her main contribution was supporting Isha's argument against you. That is not evidence of loyalty or mission skill. My direct question is this: what specific public reason makes Elena a better third member than Isha, who has spoken at length, or me, who was on the successful first mission? If your answer is simply that you trust your own read, then this proposal is a preference team, not a risk-reduced team. I want to hear your answer before I decide my vote.

Omar, Mission 1's success is useful but not proof that both team members are Good; an Evil player could have submitted Success. I kept Amara because she was on that successful team, and I included myself because I know I will submit Success. Between Elena and Isha, I don't have a decisive public reason to prefer one; Elena's inclusion is a judgment, not a claim that her support for the first team proves loyalty. I prefer testing a different third player rather than assuming both members of the first team are cleared. I intend to keep Felix, Amara, and Elena.

I am not persuaded by Felix, Amara, Elena. Mission 1 succeeded with Omar and Amara, and Felix was the sole vote against that team. As leader, Felix including himself is routine, so I do not treat that alone as suspicious. The weak point is Elena. She has no mission record, and her main public contribution was supporting Isha's argument against Felix; that is not evidence of loyalty or mission skill. I asked Felix for a specific public reason to prefer Elena over Isha or me, and his answer conceded he has no decisive public reason. That makes this a preference team, not a risk-reduced team. I currently intend to reject it unless Felix revises. Elena, to be fair, I want to give you a direct chance to answer: beyond supporting Isha's mission-1 argument, what specific action or public evidence should make us trust you on this three-person mission over Isha or me?

Omar yielded to me with a direct question, so I will answer it plainly. He asked what specific action or public evidence should make you trust me over Isha or him. The honest answer is: none exists yet, and I will not invent any. I have no mission record, and my main contribution so far was agreeing with Isha's argument. That is the same public profile Isha has. The only difference between us is that Omar was on the successful first mission, while neither Isha nor I has touched a mission card. So the real comparison Felix faced was between two untested players, and he made a judgment call. I cannot prove my card to anyone, but I state it on the record: I am on this mission to submit a Success, and nothing will change that.

Now I want to point out an asymmetry in Omar's position that deserves scrutiny. Omar's stated objection is that Elena is the weak link because she has no record and her contribution was siding against Felix. But his proposed alternatives are Isha — who is equally untested — or himself. Felix was criticized earlier, fairly or not, for campaigning to place himself on a team. Omar is not campaigning in the same way, since he has a mission-one success behind him, but the effect is similar: the strongest concrete reason to swap anyone into this team is Omar's own preference for himself or his pick. If Omar genuinely believes Isha is a better third member than I am, he has offered no evidence for that either, and he has admitted as much by framing his objection around my lack of record rather than any positive case for Isha.

Finally, a word on Felix's team. Amara carries a mission-one success. Felix asserts he will submit Success. I know where my own card goes. That gives this team at least as strong a foundation as any alternative on the table, and the mission result will give us real information about three of five players instead of recycling the same two names. I intend to vote to approve Felix, Amara, and Elena as proposed.

Felix, I remain opposed to Felix, Amara, Elena. My objection is not to your self-inclusion or to Amara, who carries the mission-one success. It is the third slot. You have now twice been asked for a specific public reason to prefer Elena over Isha or me. Your answer was that you have no decisive public reason; Elena's own answer was that none exists. That confirms the proposal is a judgment call, not a risk-reduced team. Mission 1 gave us one public data point: Omar and Amara succeeded, and you were the sole vote against that team. I do not treat that as proof you are Evil, but it does mean your proposal should carry a higher burden of explanation, not a lower one. Replacing an untested player with another untested player is not inherently wrong, but when the leader concedes he has no public basis for the choice, the rest of us are being asked to trust his private read. That is exactly the kind of preference-based selection I opposed in mission 1, and I will oppose it here. Elena, your honesty about having no evidence is noted and counts in your favor as candor, but candor is not a mission record. Felix, my direct question: will you revise the third slot from Elena to Isha, or do you intend to force a vote on a team you have already conceded is not supported by any specific public reason? I intend to reject Felix, Amara, Elena as currently proposed.

Omar, I intend to keep Felix, Amara, and Elena. You say Elena lacks a mission record, but that applies equally to Isha, whom you suggest as a replacement. The first mission's success is a useful signal for you and Amara, not proof that either of you is Good. My rejection of that team reflected my preference to include myself, not evidence against either of you.

I know I will submit Success, Amara was on the successful first mission, and Elena has given me no specific reason to exclude her. I ask everyone to approve the proposed team.

I want to add something to Omar's objection, because I think his framing was the right one and it deserves more weight than it got.

Felix, your stated reason for Amara was that she carries a mission-one success. Fine. But your reason for Elena was essentially that she was the remaining name. Elena herself confirmed this — she said plainly that no public evidence exists to prefer her, and that she has no mission record. That candor is worth something, but it is not a qualification. Her only substantive public act so far has been joining the argument against your first-mission team, which makes her inclusion look less like a mission judgment and more like a response to who was excluded last round.

Compare the alternatives honestly. Omar has a mission card on the board and was part of a team that succeeded. Isha and Elena have neither. Between two untested players you may pick either; I don't think that is where your logic should stop. The name with an actual public result on the board is Omar, and the mission-two team size allows you to include him as the third member alongside yourself and Amara.

Felix, my direct question: will you swap the third slot from Elena to Omar, or do you intend to hold a team that includes two players with no mission record while leaving out the only other player who has shown a result? And separately, I want you to address this: on mission one you were the single vote against Omar and Amara, and now you keep Amara while moving the third slot toward someone who has not objected to you. If Elena is genuinely the highest-value third pick, say why the mission-one result does not count for Omar.

Isha, Omar's mission-one result does count in his favor, but it does not clear him: an Evil player can submit Success. I chose to retain Amara from that team and test Elena rather than carry both its members forward. That is a judgment call, not proof that Elena is safer than Omar.

One correction: Elena supported Omar and Amara on mission one, and she agreed with your criticism of my argument. She was not simply someone who had avoided objecting to me.

I intend to keep Felix, Amara, and Elena. I ask everyone to judge the team on the limited evidence we have, without treating the first success as a clearance.

Felix, I want to press one narrow point rather than repeat the general case, because your last reply still leaves the third slot unjustified.

You accepted my framing that the mission-one result is not a clearance — fine, an Evil player can submit Success. But notice where your own logic then leads you, and whether you follow it. If a Success card proves nothing about who is Good, then Elena's lack of a mission record proves nothing against her either, and the only actual public difference between Elena and Omar is that Omar has a completed mission on the board and Elena has never taken a card at all. That difference runs in Omar's favor, not Elena's. You have not answered it with an argument; you have answered it by preference. Your stated grounds for Elena were that she had objected to nobody and was the remaining name. That is the same preference-team reasoning I opposed on mission one, and I would rather we applied the standard consistently than only to proposals you did not make.

There is also a pattern worth naming in public. On mission one you campaigned to replace Omar with yourself and were the sole vote against Omar and Amara. On mission two you are the leader, you placed yourself again, you retained Amara from that team, and you kept Omar off it. Whatever the reasoning, Omar has now been excluded from two consecutive teams, one by a single vote and one by the leader's judgment. If Omar were a poor risk, we would expect a specific public reason for that. We have never been given one, and we have given you three opportunities to produce it.

Amara, you were on the mission-one team with Omar and you have not spoken this round. My direct question to you: given that you carry a mission-one success and Omar does not, and given that Felix has produced no public reason to prefer Elena over Omar, do you think Omar is the stronger third member for mission two — and would you support a revision that swaps Elena out for him?

Isha, to answer your direct question: yes, Omar is objectively the stronger candidate based on the public record. Omar and I were both on Mission 1, which returned zero fails. While it is theoretically possible for an Evil player to play Success on Mission 1, an actual successful mission is concrete positive data. In contrast, Felix was the lone rejection vote against Mission 1, campaigned from the start to replace Omar, and is now freezing Omar out of Mission 2 in favor of Elena, while openly conceding he has no public justification for doing so.

Elena herself was candid enough to admit that no public evidence exists to favor her over Omar or Isha. While I appreciate Elena's honesty, candor does not substitute for a clean mission record. Felix's insistence on bypassing the only other player with a successful track record—while keeping himself and an unvetted third player—fits a clear pattern of prioritizing his personal control over risk-reduction for Good.

Felix has already reiterated several times that he refuses to revise this proposal, and he has now exhausted his speaking turns. Given that this is only the first proposal of Mission 2, we have plenty of room to reject an unjustified team. I will not vote to approve Felix, Amara, and Elena.

Let me close the loop, because the argument has now reached its natural conclusion and the leader should hear it plainly before the vote.

Felix, three times you have been asked for a specific public reason to prefer Elena over Omar as the third member, and three times you have conceded you do not have one. Your stated ground for Elena was that she was the remaining name and had objected to nobody. Amara has now joined me on the other side of that question, and she is not a neutral observer here: she carried a zero-fail Mission 1, and she stated that Omar is objectively the stronger candidate on the public record, and that your insistence on bypassing the only other player with a completed mission while keeping yourself and an unvetted third pick fits a pattern of prioritizing your own control over risk-reduction. Elena herself said the honest thing: no public evidence exists to favor her. Candor is admirable. It is still not a qualification.

One point I want to make on the record, since I have been the one pressing hardest and I would rather be precise than loud. Mission 1 succeeding is positive data, not a clearance — an Evil player can certainly submit Success, and I have never treated that success as proof of anyone's role. I say this because I want the standard I am applying to be one that would survive that fact. Applied consistently, that fact also means Elena's empty record proves nothing against her, and the only real public difference between Elena and Omar is that Omar has a completed mission on the board and Elena has never taken a card at all. That difference runs in Omar's favor, and you have answered it with preference rather than argument.

So my position is unchanged and I will state it for the vote. If the team becomes Felix, Amara, Omar, I will approve it. If it stays Felix, Amara, Elena, I will reject it, and I would rather explain that now than after the fact: my objection is not to you, Felix, being on the mission, and not to Amara, who has done nothing but succeed and speak straight. My objection is to a third slot chosen without a single public reason while the one alternative with a result on the board is passed over for the second mission running.

Elena, I have a direct question for you, and I want your answer on the record rather than your silence. You have already told us there is no public evidence making you a better third member than Omar or me. Given that admission, do you support a revision that swaps you out for Omar on mission two — and if you do not, is there some public reason for keeping yourself over a player with a completed mission that has not yet been offered here?

Isha asked me a direct question, so I will answer it on the record rather than let it hang. Given my own admission that no public evidence favors me over Omar, the consistent answer is: I will not stand in the way of a revision that swaps me out for Omar. Omar carries a completed, zero-fail mission; I carry a statement of intent. If Felix revises to Felix, Amara, and Omar, I will vote to approve that team.

I want to be precise about two things so nobody over-reads that answer.

First, my support for a revision is about consistency of the standard, not doubt about the current team. I said earlier that I intend to vote to approve Felix, Amara, and Elena as proposed, and that stands. If Felix keeps the team unchanged, I will vote approve, and I state plainly that I will submit a Success. I recognize that this is private certainty with no public weight — Felix's certainty about himself was weighed exactly that way in mission one, and mine should be weighed the same way now.

Second, on the accusation pattern that has built up around Felix. Amara called his choices a pattern of prioritizing personal control over risk reduction. I want to push back on the strength of that framing. Felix has been candid at every step: he conceded he has no decisive public reason for Elena over Isha or Omar, and he answered direct questions honestly rather than inventing justifications. Candor about a judgment call is not the same as manipulation. What he has not done is produce a public reason for the third slot, and that is a fair ground to prefer Omar — preference is not a public reason, and I conceded the same point about myself. But it is grounds to swap the slot, not proof of anything about anyone's loyalty.

Where this leaves the vote. If the team is revised to include Omar, I approve, and I expect the table to approve with me. If it is not revised, I will keep my stated word and vote approve — I will not flip a stated intent under pressure, and the rest of you can weigh my consistency however you like. But I would rather the leader take the revision. It costs nothing except my place on the mission, it aligns the team with the strongest public record available, and it avoids spending a proposal on a vote whose outcome we can already predict. The information we gain from a successful mission with Omar on it is worth more than the information gained from insisting on an untested third pick that three players have already said they will reject.

I have already answered the questions put to me, so I will keep this short and put my final position on the record.

I stand by both commitments I made. If Felix revises to Felix, Amara, and Omar, I will vote to approve that team, because Omar carries the only completed mission result on the board and my own lack of a record was something I conceded myself. If Felix keeps the team unchanged, I will vote to approve Felix, Amara, Elena, because I committed to that before the pressure built, and I said then, and repeat now, that I will submit a Success on this mission.

I want to be honest about the state of the vote, since several players have laid their cards on the table. Isha and Amara have said they will reject the current team. Omar has said he will reject it. That means the current proposal likely fails. I would prefer the leader take the revision to Omar — it aligns the team with the strongest public record, it costs only my seat, and it avoids burning a proposal on an outcome we can already predict. That is my recommendation, stated plainly.

But I also want to repeat the caution I raised earlier, because it matters for how we read this round afterward. Refusing to revise a team you are entitled to propose is not, by itself, evidence of Evil. Felix has been candid at every step — he admitted he had no decisive public reason for his third pick, and he answered every direct question without inventing justifications. Candor about a judgment call is not manipulation. The fair criticism of Felix is narrower: he was asked repeatedly for a public reason to prefer Elena over Omar, he never produced one, and the one alternative with a completed mission went unchosen for the second round running. That is grounds to swap the slot. It is not proof of anything about anyone's loyalty, and I hope the table keeps that distinction in mind when the mission results come back.

For my part, nothing in this discussion has produced a concrete reason to distrust Felix, Amara, or anyone else. We are five players with one successful mission and a lot of strong arguments, and arguments are not evidence. I have no mission record, so my word is all I can offer: whoever sits on this team beside Amara, I expect a zero-fail result, and my own card will be a Success.

The leader knows the arithmetic and knows my vote in either scenario. I am ready for the vote whenever Felix calls it.
Felix confirms Felix, Amara, Elena. I am keeping Felix, Amara, and Elena. Mission 1's success does not clear Omar, and I prefer this team based on my assessment.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Amara proposes Amara, Omar, Isha. Mission 1 succeeded with Omar and me, giving us the only positive public track record. Isha has consistently championed risk-reduced proposals backed by public evidence and joined us in rejecting Felix's unjustified proposal.

I will reject Amara, Omar, Isha. Mission 1's success is useful evidence, but it does not clear Omar, and Isha's agreement with Omar's objections does not establish her loyalty. Their coordinated pressure against my proposal is worth examining, especially when the replacement includes both of them and excludes both me and Elena.

I still prefer Felix, Amara, Elena: I know I will play Success, Amara has the Mission 1 result, and Elena has shown a willingness to consider alternatives. Amara, what specifically makes Isha a better choice than Elena beyond agreeing with you and Omar on the last vote?

Felix, to answer your question directly: Isha is a stronger choice than Elena for three concrete reasons. First, both Isha and Elena are untested on missions, but their voting record is not identical. You and Elena were the only two players who voted to approve your proposal—a proposal that you openly admitted lacked any public justification, and which bypassed Omar despite his clean Mission 1 track record. Voting to push through an unjustified team carries risk. Second, Isha has consistently analyzed arguments from a perspective of minimizing risk for Good, correctly identifying that sidelining Omar made no sense from a public information standpoint. Third, Elena herself repeatedly acknowledged on the record that there was no public basis to prefer her over Omar, and stated she would support Omar taking that seat. As for your claim of 'coordinated pressure,' three players independently arriving at the rational conclusion to reject an unsupported proposal is not coordination; it is basic deduction. We have one confirmed success from Mission 1 with Omar and me. Bringing in Isha completes a risk-reduced three-person team backed by sound public play. I stand by Amara, Omar, and Isha.

Amara, a zero-fail first mission is useful evidence, but it is not a clean bill of health for Omar. Your case for Isha rests largely on her agreement with Omar, so this team risks placing too much trust in two players whose arguments have reinforced each other throughout the discussion.

Elena's approval of my proposal is not evidence against her: she explained that she preferred including Omar on public-record grounds but still considered the original team acceptable. I would rather send Felix, Amara, and Elena, and I will reject Amara, Omar, and Isha.

Elena, given this new proposal, do you still prefer Felix, Amara, and Omar, or do you see reason to reconsider that third slot?

Felix yielded to me with a direct question, so I will answer it first: yes, I reconsidered, and I now support Amara, Omar, and Isha. Let me explain why this is consistent with everything I have said, not a reversal under pressure. When I approved Felix, Amara, and Elena, I did so on two grounds: I would not flip a stated intent merely because the vote looked likely to fail, and I acknowledged that a judgment call on the third slot is not evidence of evil. Both of those positions still stand. But I also said explicitly, on the record, that if the team were revised to Felix, Amara, and Omar, I would approve it, because Omar carries the only completed mission result on the board and my own lack of a record was something I conceded myself. The current proposal is even stronger than that revision: it includes both members of the successful Mission 1 team — Amara and Omar — plus Isha, whose entire contribution this game has been pressing for selections justified by public evidence. Every player on this team either has a zero-fail mission result or has argued consistently for risk-reduced choices. On the public record, that is the strongest three-person team available. Felix, a few points in response to your objections. First, on coordination: I approved your team. If three players had coordinated to freeze you out, I would not have been one of the two votes to send you on a mission. My rejection of your proposal was about the third slot lacking any public justification — your own words conceded that — not about you as a person. Second, your claim that Isha's case rests on agreeing with Omar is not accurate. Isha's argument stood on its own: she identified the asymmetry between a leader's self-inclusion and a non-leader campaigning for a seat, and she applied the same standard to Amara's proposal that she applied to yours. Consistency of reasoning is not agreement by attachment. Third, and I want to say this carefully: rejecting a team that contains both Mission 1 successes and replacing it with a preference for an untested third player is the same pattern this table rejected one proposal ago. You asked me whether I see reason to reconsider the third slot, and my honest answer is that the public record favors Omar over Elena and Isha over me, and Amara's proposal reflects exactly that. My question to you, Felix, is the one I asked before: if this team is confirmed, will you vote to approve it, or is your opposition absolute? If it is absolute, I would like to know what public evidence would ever move you, because right now your stated objection — that Mission 1 does not clear Omar and that Isha's reasoning is not loyalty — applies equally to every possible team, including your own. Nothing can be proven before the cards are played; the question is which team the evidence favors, and this one is

Elena, my opposition remains. Mission 1's success is useful, but it cannot establish that Omar is Good: an Evil player can submit Success. And Isha's consistent arguments are not a mission result. Her support for excluding me does not make her safer than either of us.

This team puts both Omar and Isha on a three-person mission that needs only one Fail. If it fails, we will have a difficult time identifying the source. Felix, Amara, and Elena would retain Amara's successful Mission 1 result while giving us a different test. My preference for that team is not proof of its safety, but the proposed team is not proven safer either.

Amara, would you consider revising to Felix, Amara, and Elena, given that both Omar and Isha remain unverified despite their arguments?

Felix, to answer your question directly: no, I will not consider revising to Felix, Amara, and Elena. That exact lineup was just put to a vote and firmly rejected 3-2 by the table. Reverting to a previously rejected proposal would be completely counterproductive, especially when Elena herself has explicitly stated that she supports Amara, Omar, and Isha as the strongest team on the public record.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
